review_lens: Testing & Completion Auditor — I judged the three plans only on whether their acceptance criteria are executable, branch-neutral, and sufficient to prove completion, and on whether their validation story survives contact with the actual harnesses. I re-derived every claim below from source or executed output; I did not evaluate plan structure, sequencing elegance, or security merit except where a criterion depends on it.
blocking_issues: BLOCKING — The A-1 acceptance criterion in all three plans is fix-branch-dependent and therefore not executable across a decision the contract deliberately leaves open. All three assert the viewer 'selects from cw.session and gets zero rows' (Planner A WP-D; Planner B acceptance item 7; Planner C A-1 criterion). Observed: under the actor-scoped-policy option the grant at backend/db/migrations/0032_session_store.sql:28 survives and the select returns zero rows; under the dedicated-lookup-role option the grant is revoked and the same select raises psycopg.errors.InsufficientPrivilege. backend/doorway/db.py has no wrapping that converts a denied SELECT into an empty result (SilentlyRefused at db.py:132-147 covers write_one only), so the test ERRORS rather than passing under the option two of the three plans recommend. Contract success criterion 5 makes this choice approval-sensitive and undecided at Gate 2; an acceptance criterion that only passes on one branch cannot be written into a package before the branch is chosen. Must be restated branch-neutrally: the viewer obtains no session row, whether by refusal or by empty result — and the same for the delete.
major_defects: MAJOR (Planner A, WP-H) — WP-H's acceptance criterion cannot pass, and A scopes the package as 'test-only and additive'. A's criterion: 'as an ordinary requester, a direct select using another deal's identifier returns zero rows or is refused.' Observed at backend/db/migrations/0005_run_store.sql:288-295: `grant select, insert on cw.snapshot, cw.snapshot_member, cw.snapshot_ladder_rung, cw.ruleset, cw.ruleset_member … to cw_requester, cw_legal_reviewer, cw_legal_admin` plus a select grant to cw_auditor; lines 265-268 enable RLS on cw.run, cw.run_decision and cw.run_finding ONLY. A requester therefore CAN select those rows directly today. The criterion fails against correct, unfixed code, so WP-H as written either stalls or silently forces the schema change A lists as optional investigation. Planner C (WP-B4a) is the only plan that identifies this and specifies the achievable form — a source-shape test asserting no module composes a caller-supplied id against those tables without resolving through cw.run.

MAJOR (Planner A WP-D/WP-I, Planner B WP-8) — Both plans propose an import that is circular and would fail at import time. A's WP-D: 'replace the five literals with the imported constant' (identity.LOOKUP_ACTOR). B's WP-8: 'Route the five literals through LOOKUP_ROLE.' Observed: backend/doorway/identity.py:48 already does `from doorway.sessions import EIGHT_HOURS, Sessions, parse_duration`, and backend/doorway/sessions.py imports nothing from identity.py (grep: no import). sessions.py importing identity.py closes the cycle. Planner A states the cycle was 'verified not to create a cycle' — that verification is scoped to db.py (correct for `Database`, since db.py imports only stdlib and psycopg) and does not cover identity.py, which is the module A's own WP-D names. Planner B compounds it by making a sequencing decision on top ('WP-8 should be pulled forward and sequenced BEFORE WP-5' so that WP-5's Python surface collapses to one site). Planner C is clean here: WP-B8 proposes only the Database import and the threading removal.

MAJOR (Planner B, WP-6) — B9's scope in Planner B misses the third cluster-wide write, so the package's acceptance criterion could pass by luck while a live collision source remains. B scopes 'the retry-once wrapper on setup.py:39 and the 0016 DO block'. Observed at backend/db/migrations/0016_doorway_login.sql:45-47: `grant cw_viewer, cw_requester, cw_legal_reviewer, cw_legal_admin, cw_auditor, cw_administrator to cw_app;` sits OUTSIDE the DO block, is unconditional, and writes pg_auth_members on every per-test schema rebuild (backend/doorway/conftest.py rebuilds from the migrations per test). Planners A (WP-F) and C (EV-013) both name it. A B9 package scoped from B's text would leave a rarer, harder-to-attribute version of the same failure and would still report green on a concurrency test that is inherently probabilistic.

MAJOR (all three plans, B2) — The B2 acceptance criterion has no discriminator and is therefore either unfilterable or false-passing. A: 'assert from an independent connection that zero backends are idle-in-transaction while it blocks'; B: 'reports ZERO idle-in-transaction backends'; C: 'zero idle in transaction backends attributable to the serving pool'. Observed at backend/doorway/db.py:164-173: ConnectionPool is constructed with min_size/max_size and `kwargs={'autocommit': True}` and sets NO application_name. The test harness's own fixtures connect to the same database as the same login (backend/doorway/conftest.py), so pg_stat_activity cannot distinguish a serving-pool backend from the test's own. C's qualifier names the right property but supplies no mechanism. The criterion needs a concrete discriminator — capture the pool connection's pid via `select pg_backend_pid()` inside as_person, or set application_name on the pool — or it will pass whether or not B2 is fixed.
minor_defects: MINOR (Planner B) — Stale-row arithmetic is inconsistent and would mis-scope WP-0. Executed `doorway.mutation_check.preflight()` against the working tree: it returns FIVE entries over FOUR distinct rows — the row 'removing an expired session crashes if another request removed it first' trips twice, once for the missing pattern in doorway/sessions.py and once for naming test_sessions.py::test_an_entry_removed_mid_check_is_no_session_not_a_crash, which does not exist. Planner B says 'four rows' in WP-0 but 'the 5 stale rows' in its risks and '5 stale entries' in acceptance. Planners A and C both count four rows. A WP-0 acceptance criterion phrased in rows must say four; phrased in preflight output lines it must say five.

MINOR (all three plans) — No plan's mutation-row obligation mentions the uniqueness rule, which is the second way an edit turns the gate red. Observed at backend/doorway/mutation_check.py:495-500: preflight appends a stale entry not only when hits == 0 but also when hits > 1 ('pattern appears N times … it would mutate the first, which may be the wrong one'). Every plan adds new mutation rows (B1 guard, A-1 policy, B2 placement) and edits source that other rows pin verbatim. A new find-string that is not unique, or a product edit that duplicates an existing pinned string, fails the gate identically to a deleted one. The per-package checklist must say 'unique and present', not just 'present'.

MINOR (Planner A WP-J, Planner C recurrence guard) — Both criteria assume an engine preflight that does not exist. Executed: `engine.mutation_check` raises AttributeError for `preflight`; grep of backend/engine/mutation_check.py shows staleness is detected only inside _run_one (line 515-516, `if find not in src: return … 'skip'`) and scored at line 554-556. The engine harness therefore discovers a stale row only by running all 57 mutations, each a full pytest subprocess. A's 'engine/mutation_check.py still reports 0 stale' and C's 'run the mutation harnesses' preflight early in npm run verify (a pure text check that takes seconds)' both need either the ad-hoc probe named as a package deliverable or a preflight written for the engine harness — neither is scoped by any plan.

MINOR (Planner A) — An evidence gap that A discounts its own confidence for. A reports 'I could not read package.json — it is absent or empty at the repository root' and carries the Unresolved question 'Is npm run verify in fact wired to both mutation harnesses?'. Observed: backend/package.json exists and answers it — `"test:mutation": "node db/test/mutation-check.mjs && python engine/mutation_check.py && python doorway/mutation_check.py"` and `"verify": "npm run test && npm run test:engine && npm run test:doorway && npm run test:mutation"`. A also missed the third harness (db/test/mutation-check.mjs), which C flags as unchecked for staleness and which no plan probes.

MINOR (Planner B, B9 acceptance) — 'the serial second pass … becomes unnecessary and can be removed' is not a valid test of B9's fix and would weaken the harness. Observed at backend/doorway/mutation_check.py:519-537 and 570-577: the second pass re-runs every row whose verdict is `imprecise`, i.e. the suite failed but NOT through the named test. The comment attributes the common case to rebuild collisions but the verdict class is broader — any fixture failure produces it. Deleting the retry converts a safety net into a proof obligation and re-creates precisely the condition the comment records ('nine guarantees reported as guarded that were never evaluated at all').

MINOR (Planners A and B, B9) — Only Planner C requires the B9 reproduction to be seen to fail against the pre-fix code. A's criterion is 'two pytest processes … both complete without tuple concurrently updated'; B's is the same. A concurrency race can produce a green run by luck, so a post-fix-only criterion proves nothing. The repository's own standard is stated in backend/doorway/mutation_check.py's header — a guarantee must have been seen to fail — and C applies it consistently ('the test is shown to fail against the pre-fix code') where A and B do not.

MINOR (Planner B, WP-4) — Silent scope creep on B4's table count, with a criterion that matches neither source. bug_report.md:124-137 names five tables in prose while its own quoted pg_class output lists seven (adding audit_checkpoint and schema_migration). B scopes six (folding in audit_checkpoint) and its acceptance criterion reads 'for each of the six tables PostgreSQL reports without RLS' — the query reports seven, not six. audit_checkpoint is part of the audit chain, which hard constraint 5 pins as append-only; adding it to a B4 package that may end in RLS policies is a scope and risk change that must be argued, not absorbed.

MINOR (Planner C, B3 traceability) — C removes B3 from the package set entirely ('Escalation, not a package') and its acceptance-criteria list gives B3 only the negative 'no test is weakened'. Contract success criterion 1 permits explicit, justified deferral and C's justification is sound (verified: backend/engine/test_manifest.py:112-125 asserts `checked.coerced == ()` for 'HIGH'/'high'/' High ' with the stated rationale). But a deferral recorded only as a bullet inside proposed_actions will not appear in a work-package traceability matrix. A and B both give B3 a numbered decision package; C should too, even if it contains no code.
unsupported_claims: Planner A: 'The doorway mutation harness is what npm run verify invokes … I could not read package.json — it is absent or empty at the repository root, so the wiring is not directly Observed.' Disconfirmed as an evidence gap: backend/package.json exists and states the wiring. The conclusion is right; the claim of unavailability is not.

Planner A, WP-I: 'add `from doorway.db import Database` — verified not to create a cycle, since db.py imports nothing from sessions.py.' The stated verification is sound for db.py and does NOT support A's separate WP-D proposal to import identity.LOOKUP_ACTOR into sessions.py, which is a cycle (identity.py:48 imports doorway.sessions). The verification is presented as covering the sessions.py import work generally.

Planner B: 'Statically checked engine/mutation_check.py: 57 mutations, 0 stale.' The count of 57 is confirmed, but the harness exposes no preflight (AttributeError on engine.mutation_check.preflight), so 'statically checked' must mean an ad-hoc probe B does not describe. Its result is plausible but the method is not reproducible from the report, which matters because B makes 'zero stale patterns across both harnesses' a per-package acceptance criterion.

Planner B, WP-5: '(the minimal fix) is correctly described as needing no Python change — sessions.py:87, 112, 119, 130, 134 all open with as_person(\'__signin__\', \'viewer\').' The line references are confirmed exactly. But B elsewhere describes these same five sites as 'five hardcoded \'viewer\' literals bypassing LOOKUP_ROLE' — they hardcode BOTH literals, and identity.py:57/62 defines both LOOKUP_ROLE and LOOKUP_ACTOR. B's WP-8 addresses only the role literal; Planner A's WP-D addresses only the actor literal. Neither plan states that both constants are bypassed at the same five sites.

Planner B, WP-6 acceptance: 'doorway/mutation_check.py's serial second pass (lines 524-546) becomes unnecessary and can be removed without lanes dying in their fixture.' No evidence supports that role collision is the ONLY producer of the `imprecise` verdict; the code at mutation_check.py:570-577 defines it as any suite failure not routed through the named test.
missed_risks: No plan states how a package proves its NEW mutation row was seen to fail. Every plan adds rows (B1 guard, A-1 policy, B2 placement) and every plan asserts 'the harness exits 0'. Exiting 0 proves the row's pattern is present, unique, and that the named test failed under mutation — but only if the row's mutation is genuinely behaviour-changing. A row whose replacement text is a no-op still scores `miss`, not `ok`, so the failure mode is caught; a row whose named test fails for an unrelated reason scores `imprecise`. The plans should require the new row's verdict to be `ok` specifically, not merely a zero exit for the run.

Feasibility of a SQL mutation row is unprecedented but I confirmed it works — worth recording so the integrator does not drop C's A-1 criterion as unbuildable. Observed: 0 of 36 doorway rows target a .sql file (all target doorway/*.py). But _run_one at mutation_check.py:414-419 copies db/migrations into the temp tree, and doorway/migrate.py:35-36 resolves MIGRATIONS_DIR from `Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / 'db' / 'migrations'`, which inside the temp tree points at the copy. A mutated migration is therefore the one applied by the per-test rebuild. C's 'a mutation row that restores the unscoped grant requires that test to fail' is buildable; it just has no precedent and should be costed as first-of-kind.

The doorway suite's per-process database means the mutation harness runs each row in its own database, which is why B9's collision is specifically about CLUSTER-wide role state and cannot be fixed by more isolation. Observed at backend/doorway/conftest.py:44-56: TEST_DATABASE defaults to `clausewerk_doorway_{os.getpid()}`, and each _run_one spawns a fresh pytest subprocess with its own pid. No plan states this explicitly, and a package owner reading B9's diagnosis could reasonably propose 'give each run its own database' as the fix — which is already done and would waste the package.

Planner C's B1 unit criterion is executable but has an unstated boundary. Observed: Write.bind (backend/doorway/writes.py:133-152) is database-free, and test_writes.py:177/290/303 already parametrizes over sorted(WRITES) without the schema fixture, so C's DB-free criterion is sound. But bind's blankness test is `value is None or str(value).strip() == ""` — `str({})` is '{}' and `str([])` is '[]', neither blank — so the new shape guard interacts with, rather than replaces, the blankness path, and a criterion that only tests non-empty dicts leaves the empty-dict case unpinned. Exactly one field in the whole write table is as_json=True (writes.py:298, Field('findings', as_json=True)), so the exemption arm of the parametrized test has a single case and should be named rather than left implicit.

No plan's acceptance criteria address what happens to the four stale mutation rows' GUARANTEES, only to the rows. Three of them concern session expiry, sweeping, and delete-races. If WP-0/WP-A/WP-T0 repoints them at the database-backed store, the repointing itself needs the seen-to-fail demonstration; if it retires them, three guarantees leave the suite. Planner C is the only plan that raises retirement as an open question; A and B both assume repointing is possible without checking that an equivalent database-backed guarantee exists.
recommended_corrections: Restate the A-1/D-1 acceptance criterion branch-neutrally before any package is authored: 'a person holding the viewer role obtains no row from cw.session and removes none — whether the database refuses the statement or returns an empty result.' Assert on row count OR on an InsufficientPrivilege being raised, never on either alone, and never on message text. This is the only correction that must land before Gate 3.

Replace Planner A's WP-H acceptance criterion with Planner C's WP-B4a formulation (a source-shape test that no module composes a caller-supplied identifier against the five tables without resolving through cw.run), and move any RLS work to a separately-budgeted package as C's WP-B4b does. Cite 0005_run_store.sql:288-295 in the package so the next reader does not re-propose the behavioural test.

Strike the sessions.py-imports-identity.py step from Planner A's WP-D and Planner B's WP-8, or invert it: move LOOKUP_ROLE and LOOKUP_ACTOR into a module both sessions.py and identity.py may import (or into sessions.py itself, which identity.py already imports). Remove B's WP-8-before-WP-5 sequencing rationale, which rests on the unworkable version.

Add `grant cw_viewer, … to cw_app` at 0016_doorway_login.sql:45-47 to Planner B's WP-6 scope; require the B9 package to enumerate all three cluster-wide statements and to demonstrate the reproduction failing against pre-fix code, per Planner C's formulation.

Give the B2 criterion a discriminator: capture the serving connection's `pg_backend_pid()` inside db.as_person for the duration of the probe (or set application_name on the pool at db.py:165) and assert on pg_stat_activity filtered to that pid. Without one, the criterion cannot distinguish the pool from the test's own fixtures.

Add to every package's definition of done, in the words of the harness rather than the plan: each new or repointed mutation row must be present exactly once in its target file (mutation_check.py:495-500 fails on hits > 1 as well as hits == 0), must name a test that exists, and must return verdict `ok` — not merely leave the run's exit code at 0.

Name the ad-hoc stale-pattern probe as a deliverable, or scope a preflight() for engine/mutation_check.py. Both A's WP-J criterion and C's recurrence guard currently reference a capability the engine harness does not have. Also probe the third harness, db/test/mutation-check.mjs, which no plan has checked for staleness and which npm run test:mutation runs first.

Give B3 a numbered decision package in Planner C's plan even though it contains no code, so it survives into the traceability matrix under contract success criterion 1. Reconcile B4's table count across all three plans against the pg_class output (seven tables, five in scope per bug_report.md's prose) and state explicitly whether audit_checkpoint is in or out, given hard constraint 5.

Reconcile the stale-count wording: four rows, five preflight entries. Any WP-0/WP-A/WP-T0 acceptance criterion should assert `preflight() == []` rather than a count, which removes the ambiguity entirely.
